titulo: Validate a keyword without a paid tool
lead: Writing about what nobody searches for is wasted work; so is writing about what every big portal already owns. Before you open the editor, score each keyword with free signals: autocomplete, Google Trends, Search Console, and the search results themselves. And only move forward if you have something real to say.
objetivo: score 10 keywords with the GO/NO-GO score and group the approved ones by intent, each group with one owner page.

aprende.t: The free sources and what each one tells you
The GO / MAYBE / NO-GO score, criterion by criterion
Group keywords by intent in a spreadsheet
The honest limit of the free tools and when a paid one helps

hero_alt: A person at the kitchen table sorts paper cards into two piles, with a laptop beside them.

secoes.titulo: From raw list to approved content plan

nos.detalhe: Customer questions, doubts from your community, queries already showing up in Search Console, suggestions from an AI assistant. Quantity is good here: the filter comes later.
Each source gives a partial signal. A suggestion in autocomplete = someone searches for it. An impression in Search Console = you already show up. The top 10 shows whether you can compete.
Each criterion adds or subtracts points. The criterion that weighs the most: you have an experiment, course, project, or real data to cite (+2; without it, −3).
GO goes into the content plan. MAYBE goes in only if there's room. NO-GO is out, even if the keyword looks good.
Approved keywords are grouped by intent. Each group becomes ONE owner page (lesson 2), and the variations become sections of it, not new pages.

secoes.legenda: Without first-hand data, the score drops three points: that's how the score separates your content from non-commodity content.

secoes.titulo: Score a keyword in five looks

texto: Type the start of the search into Google, in an incognito window. If the phrase shows up as a suggestion, someone searches for it.
Repeat with letters after the term ("how to make bread a", "b"...) to collect real variations.
In Google Trends, compare with an anchor term you know. Interest above zero over 12 months: +2. At least 10% of the anchor: +3.
Zero over 12 months is a NO-GO signal, no matter how much you like the idea.
If the query already has an impression in your Search Console, at any position, it earns the highest point: it's confirmed demand for your site.
A query with impressions and no dedicated page is a content-plan topic validated for free (course 3 goes deeper).
Open the top 10. At least 3 weak results (forum, video without text, old page, another language): +2.
Top 10 dominated by big platforms with a page specific to the search: −2. Intent to learn or buy: +1.

secoes.titulo: The score spreadsheet and the grouping request
secoes.sub: Copy it into your spreadsheet. The grouping can be done by an agent on your subscription, with your review.

blocos.conteudo:
| Criterion | Points |
|---|---|
| Shows up in Google autocomplete | +2 |
| Google Trends > 0 over 12 months (≥ 10% of an anchor term: +3) | +2 |
| Already has impressions in Search Console | +3 |
| Intent to learn or buy | +1 |
| Top 10 with ≥ 3 weak results (forum, video with no text, old, other language) | +2 |
| Top 10 dominated by big platforms with a specific page | −2 |
| You have a real experiment/course/project to cite | +2 (without it: −3) |

GO ≥ 6 · MAYBE 3–5 · NO-GO ≤ 2

abas.html:
Fictional example, from a sourdough bakery:

  • "como fazer levain": autocomplete +2, Trends +3, no impressions 0, learning +1, top 10 with 3 weak results +2, recipe tested at the bakery itself +2 → 10, GO.
  • "melhor pão do Brasil": autocomplete +2, Trends +2, no impressions 0, no clear intent 0, big portals −2, nothing first-hand −3 → −1, NO-GO.

Exact search volume doesn't exist for free. Google Ads Keyword Planner, in an account with no campaign, shows only ranges (10–100, 100–1K).

Paid tools (DataForSEO, Semrush, Ahrefs) give numbers and difficulty. They're optional: check the price on each site. The score above decides without them.

secoes.sub: A spreadsheet with the template's columns.

exercicios.texto: Build a list of 10 terms from your topic and score each one with the five checks. In the "dado próprio" column, write which experiment, product, or real case you would cite.
exercicios.pronto: the spreadsheet has 10 rows with a score and a decision, and every GO row has its first-hand data described.

exercicios.texto: Group the GO terms by intent (by hand or with the request to the agent) and check the result. Cross-check with the canonical map from lesson 2.
exercicios.pronto: each group has one main keyword and one owner page, and no group produced two pages.

secoes.sub: The explanation shows up after your answer.

perguntas.p: A term adds up to 7 points, but you have no case or first-hand data to cite. What is the real score?
opcoes: It loses the +2 and gets −3, and drops to MAYBE or NO-GO.
You can't know without a paid tool.
perguntas.explica: The first-hand data criterion is what separates your content from commodity content. Without it, the page would be the same as the others.

perguntas.p: Which signal is worth the most points?
opcoes: Already having impressions in your Search Console.
perguntas.explica: Impressions in your own Search Console are confirmed demand for your site: +3.

perguntas.p: Five approved keywords have the same intent. How many pages?
opcoes: One owner page; the variations become sections.
perguntas.explica: One page per keyword variation is the shortcut that turns into cannibalization and scaled content.

perguntas.p: What can you learn for free about search volume?
opcoes: Signals and ranges: autocomplete, relative Trends, Keyword Planner ranges, and your own impressions.
perguntas.explica: Exact volume is a paid-tool thing. The free signals are enough to decide GO or NO-GO.

itens.texto: Autocomplete, Trends, Search Console, top 10, and your own first-hand data.
MAYBE only if there's room left; NO-GO is out.
Variations become sections of the owner page.
Google's guide for AI says non-commodity content is what counts: the first-hand data point is the criterion that weighs the most.
